Gainsay
GAYN-say
v.
Old English gēan- (against) + secgan (to say): literally to say-against. Renders the Greek antilegō, “to speak against, contradict, oppose in words.”

📖 Biblical Definition

To gainsay is to speak against—to contradict, oppose, deny, refute. The Old English construction is precise (gain-, against; -say, speak), and the KJV uses the verb to render the Greek antilegō in contexts where the contradiction is verbal and public. Christ promises His witnesses such a gift of utterance that all your adversaries shall not be able to gainsay nor resist (Luke 21:15)—the apostolic word will be such that opponents cannot effectively contradict it. Titus 1:9 sets the verb at the qualifications for elders: the bishop must be holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers—the gainsayers being those who actively speak against sound apostolic doctrine. Romans 10:21 uses the verb of Israel’s long history of resisting God’s pleading: all day long I have stretched forth my hands unto a disobedient and gainsaying people. Jude 11 names the gainsaying of Core—Korah’s contradiction of Moses’ appointed leadership and presumption against the Aaronic priesthood, ending in his and his company being swallowed alive by the earth (Num 16). The verb’s biblical pattern therefore traces three uses: the gainsaying of unbelievers against the gospel (which Christ promises His witnesses shall not prevail); the gainsaying of false teachers against sound doctrine (which the elder must refute by sound doctrine); and the gainsaying of the rebellious against God’s appointed leadership (which incurs severe judgment). To gainsay is therefore not merely to disagree but to set one’s speech actively against what God has spoken, established, or commissioned—a serious verb for a serious posture, and one that the KJV retains in its full Anglo-Saxon weight where modern translations often soften it.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines GAINSAY as to contradict; to oppose in words; to deny or declare not to be true what another has said.

expand to see more

GAINSAY, v.t. — To contradict; to oppose in words; to deny or declare not to be true what another has said; to controvert. Adversaries shall not be able to gainsay nor resist (Luke 21:15).

GAINSAYER, n. — One who contradicts or denies what is alleged; an opposer. That he may be able...to convince the gainsayers (Tit 1:9).

📖 Key Scripture

Luke 21:15 — "For I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which all your adversaries shall not be able to gainsay nor resist."

Titus 1:9 — "Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers."

Romans 10:21 — "But to Israel he saith, All day long I have stretched forth my hands unto a disobedient and gainsaying people."

Jude 1:11 — "Woe unto them! for they have gone in the way of Cain, and ran greedily after the error of Balaam for reward, and perished in the gainsaying of Core."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Gainsay is corrupted by the modernizing impulse that has replaced the precise KJV vocabulary with the colorless contradict or oppose—losing the Anglo-Saxon weight of say-against—and by the contemporary collapse of the very category of speaking-against-God’s-Word that the verb names, in a culture where every assertion is treated as one valid opinion among many.

expand to see more

Modernizing translations have widely replaced gainsay with the colorless contradict, oppose, or argue against. The replacement is grammatically defensible; the loss is rhetorical and pastoral. Gainsay carries the Anglo-Saxon directness of say-against: it names a speech-act of active verbal opposition, with weight, with risk, with seriousness. Contradict in modern usage has been domesticated into the polite register of academic disagreement; gainsay still carries the older weight of Korah’s rebellion and the gospel-opponent’s public defiance. The KJV’s retention of the word is therefore not archaism for its own sake but the preservation of a vocabulary register that the modern equivalents have lost. Readers who learn to hear the KJV in its own idiom recover access to a register of speech-seriousness that the modern translations, for all their accessibility, have inadvertently flattened.

The deeper contemporary corruption is the collapse of the very category the verb names. Gainsay requires a fixed standard against which the contradiction is measured—God’s Word, sound doctrine, the appointed leadership. In a culture where every assertion is treated as one valid opinion among many, no claim has the standing to be gainsaid: there is only the endless equivalence of competing views. Scripture refuses this. There is a faithful word which is to be held fast; there is sound doctrine by which gainsayers are to be convinced; there is God’s pleading at which Israel’s gainsaying was judged; there are appointed offices and ordinances which Korah’s gainsaying could not overturn. Recover both ends: the precise vocabulary that names the speech-act, and the substantive standards (Word, doctrine, leadership) without which the speech-act has no biblical referent. The elder who can convince the gainsayers by sound doctrine is the elder Titus 1:9 requires, and the church saturated with such elders is the church that holds its faithful word across the centuries against every contradiction.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old English gēan- (against) + secgan (to say) — literally say-against; renders Greek antilegō, the verbal opposition that contradicts God’s Word, sound doctrine, or appointed leadership.

expand to see more

Greek antilegō (G483) — to speak against, contradict, oppose in words (Luke 2:34; 21:15; John 19:12; Acts 13:45; 28:19, 22; Rom 10:21; Tit 1:9; 2:9).

Greek antilogia (G485) — the act of speaking against, contradiction, dispute (Heb 6:16; 7:7; 12:3; Jude 11, “the gainsaying of Core”).

Old English gēan- — against (the prefix giving the verb its directional sense).

Old English secgan — to say (the root of modern say).
